Meeting Schedule

The regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month,
closed session business will usually commence at 5:30 p.m., when scheduled, and general business
session will commence at 6:30 p.m.

Brown Act

Agendas are drafted to accurately state what the legislative body is being asked to consider. The
legislative body can take action on "all items" listed on the agenda and be in compliance with the open
meeting laws. Under the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the
agenda, or unless certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The governing body may direct
staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for consideration at a future meeting.

City's Vision Statement

We envision a thriving, safe and inclusive community where everyone has the opportunity to access
exceptional services, education and support to be resilient and live full, vibrant lives.

Public Communications

Public Comments on agenda items are limited to three (3) minutes. All comments are to be addressed
directly to the Agency Members not to the members of the public.

Emails for public comment received prior to 12pm on the day of the Council Meeting will be summarized
by the City Clerk, not read in its entirety. A copy of the email will be provided to the City Council and will
also be available at the City Clerk's Office for public review. A copy of each email will be recorded for
public record and noted on the official minutes of tonight's meeting.

Meeting Compensation Disclosure
Pursuant to Government Code Section 54952.3: Disclosure of compensation for meeting
attendance by City Council Members is $790 monthly regardless of the amount of meetings.

Comments From The Audience - Non-Agenda Items
During this time, members of the public may address the City Council regarding any items not
listed on the agenda and within the subject matter jurisdiction of the City Council and not on
this agenda. Comments from the audience will be limited to three (3) minutes per speaker;
unless authorized by the Mayor, the time limit may not be extended by utilizing another
member's time. There will be no debate or action on items not listed on the agenda unless
authorized by law. The collective initial period of time for comments from the audience shall
be limited to 45 minutes. Any speaker that did not get a chance to speak during this segment
due to the 45-minute limitations will be able to speak at the end of the meeting prior to
adjournment.

Note: The City Council desires to provide all members of the public with the opportunity to
address the Council. Nevertheless, obscene language, comments intended to
disrupt/interfere, other actions which disrupt the progress of the meeting or slanderous
comments will not be tolerated and may result in ejection and/or may constitute a violation of
South Gate Municipal Code Section1.04.110.

Reports And Comments From City Officials
During this time, members of the City Council will report on matters pertaining to their service
on various intergovernmental boards and commissions as a representative of the City
pursuant to Assembly Bill 1234. City Council Members will also have an opportunity to
comment on matters not on the agenda.

Consent Calendar Items

Agenda Items 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 are Consent Calendar Items. All items including
Ordinances, Resolutions and Contracts, may be approved by adoption of the Consent
Calendar, individually and collectively by one (1) motion. There will be no separate discussion
of these items unless Members of the City Council, the public, or staff request that specific
items be removed from the Consent Calendar for separate discussion and action. Members
of the public are permitted to speak on any item listed but their time period is limited to three
(3) minutes in total.

Any motion to introduce or adopt an Ordinance on the Consent Calendar shall be: (1) a
motion to waive the reading of the Ordinance and introduce the Ordinance or (2) a motion to
waive the reading of the Ordinance and adopt the Ordinance, as appropriate.

 GENERAL NOTICE TO THE PUBLIC

The City Council adopted new rules relating to the conduct of the public meetings, proceedings, and
business in the City of South Gate on July 12, 2022, (Resolution 2022-38-CC) and go into effect on
August 1, 2022. Resolution #2022-38-CC is available at the City Clerk’s Office.

MEETING SCHEDULE

Regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month, closed
session meetings will commence at 5:30 p.m. unless posted otherwise on its agenda. The regular City
Council meetings will commence at 6:30 p.m. Agendas are available at the following locations: City Clerk
Office, Public Notice Boards at City Hall, and on the City’s web page at https://www.cityofsouthgate.org

The Public can sign up to receive automatic notices of postings of agendas for the City Council or any
other Commission or Board of the City of South Gate. Visit the City webpage and click on the Agenda &
Minutes icon. That will take you the page where an individual can enter their email in the “Email
Updates” box to register.

PUBLIC COMMENT/PARTICIPATION

Any person may request to address a legislative body during a public meeting. The Presiding Officer will
call upon those present in the Council Chambers first. After all speakers in the Chambers have spoken,
the Presiding Officer will call upon those participating via zoom or teleconference.

Speakers are limited to three (3) minutes on any item listed on the agenda, including public hearings.
Under Comments from the Audience portion, speakers are also limited to a single three (3) minutes time
limit. Comments from the Audience is initially limited to 45 minutes at each meeting. Any speaker still
wishing to speak, that did not speak, will have an addition Comments from the Audience opportunity after
the last business item is finished. The Presiding Officer may extend the time limit as long as there is no
objection from the City Council as a body.

To ensure that the public is able to participate, the City provides the opportunity to submit their
comments in person, virtually, email, phone call, mail and any other method which may become
available. Methods of participation may be subject to change during other such times when a State of
Emergency, Health Order or State Executive Order limits in-person participation.

CURFEW

In absence of a motion duly adopted by majority vote of the City Council, the Presiding Officer may
adjourn the City Council meetings at 10:30 p.m. The Presiding Officer may ask the City Council if any
agenda items listed should be continued or dealt with during the meeting. For those items to be
continued, the City Council can direct the item be placed on the next City Council agenda or the current
meeting may be adjourned to a time certain at which time the meeting shall be reconvened as an
Adjourned Regular Meeting of the City Council and action upon the published agenda continued.

STAFF REPORTS

As a general rule, staff reports. or other written documentation are prepared/organized with respect to
each item of business listed on the agenda. Meeting agendas and staff reports are available at least 72-
hours prior to the scheduled regular City Council meeting and a minimum of 24-hours prior to a Special
City Council meeting. There are times when the City Council receives written material. revised material
after the posting of agendas, these materials are become a public record and will be available for public
view within 72-hours after the meeting in which they were received. Those materials and any other public
document can be inspected in the City Clerk's Office located at 8650 California Avenue, South Gate.

  7
 SERVICES TO FACILITATE ACCESS TO PUBLIC MEETINGS

In compliance with the American with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in the
City Council Meetings, please contact the Office of the City Clerk. Notification 48 hours prior to the City
Council Meeting will enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to assure accessibility. For
further information, please contact the Office of the City Clerk at (323) 563-9510 or via email at
yglaze@sogate.org.

SUBJECT:  INTRODUCTION  AND FIRST READING  OF ORDINANCE  AUTHORIZING
AN AMENDMENT  TO THE CALIFORNIA  PUBLIC EMPLOYEES'  RETIREMENT  SYSTEM
CONTRACT  TO IMPLEMENT  A COST SHARING  PROGRAM  BETWEEN  THE CITY AND
UNREPRESENTED  EXECUTIVE  MANAGEMENT  CONTRACT  EMPLOYEES  GROUP

PURPOSE:  To introduce an Ordinance authorizing an amendment to the contract with the California
Public Employees Retirement System ("CalPERS") to implement a cost sharing program  amendment
between the City of South Gate ("City") and the Board of Administration of the CalPERS to implement
a cost sharing program between the Unrepresented Executive Management Contract Employees group
("Executives").

RECOMMENDED  ACTION:  The City Council will consider waiving  the reading in full and
introducing an Ordinance authorizing an amendment to the contract between the City and the Board of
Administration  of the California Public Employees' Retirement System implementing Section 20516
(Employees Sharing Additional Cost) to provide employee cost sharing of 1% for Executives effective
on December  31, 2023.

FISCALIMPACT:  Theestimatedsavingsfromimplementingthecostsharingprogramis$17,600in
Fiscal Year 2023-2024 and an additional$l79,000  in Fiscal Year 2024-25.

NOTICING  REQUIREMENTS:  A public hearing notice was duly published in the South Gate Press,
a newspaper of general circulation  on Thursday, October 19, 2023.

ANALYSIS:  California retirement law allows for two types of cost sharing (where employees pay a
portion of the employer contribution to CalPERS). The first type of cost sharing is by CalPERS contract
amendment under Government Code (GC) § 20516(a-e). In order for cost sharing to be effective under
that method, CalPERS must first approve a contract amendment with the City. This form of cost sharing
is generally more favorable for employees, as the additional employee contributions are considered by
CalPERS to be "normal member contributions"  and are treated as pre-tax contributions. As such, this is
the cost-sharing  method  the City is proposing.

The alternative method is cost sharing under GC Eg20516(f). That methodology is between the City and
its employees only, without a CalPERS contract amendment. Under GC § 20516(f), the additional
employee contributions effectively subsidize the City's CalPERS contributions and are considered as
after-tax  contributions.

BACKGROUND:  The City's current contract with CalPERS provides that all employees pay the full
employee share toward their retirement benefit. That contribution percentage differs based on whether
they are "Classic"  unit members or "PEPRA"  unit members. During the most recent contract
  9
  1
 negotiations  between  the City  and the Executives,  they  agreed  tliat  they  would  participate  in a cost
sharing  program.  The South  Gate Police  Management  Association  ("SGPMA")  was the first labor group
to participate  in the cost sharing  program  by having  all their "Classic"  unit  members  contribute  2% of
their  salary  toward  the City's  share of their  retirement  benefits  beginning  in FY  2022-23.  The  final
ordinance  amending  the CalPERS  contract  for the cost sharing  program  with  SGPMA  was approved  by
the City  Council  at its February  14, 2023, meeting.

The other employee  associations,  the Miscellaneous  Employees'  Association  ("MEA"),  the Professional
Mid-Management  Association  ("PMMA"),  the Division  Management  Association  ("DMA"),  and the
Police  Officers'  Association  ("POA"),  followed  with  members  agreeing  to participate  in the cost sharing
program  by contributing  1% of their salary toward  the City's  share of their retirement  benefits  beginning
in FY 2023-24.  The final  ordinance  amending  the CalPERS  contract  for the cost sharing  program  with
MEA,  PMMA,  DMA,  and POA  was approved  by the City  Council  at its June 13, 2023,  meeting.  The
cost sharing program for each of these labor groups  is pursuant  to California  Governi'nent  Code 20516(a)
and was effective in July 2023.

Staff  began  working  with  CalPERS  to amend  the City's  contract  to implement  this change  in August
2023 and received  approval  and the necessary  information  to move  forward  on September  6, 2023.

The cost sharing  arrangement  has already  been approved  by the City  Council  on September  13, 2022,
by a resolution  approving  the updated  salary  tables  and benefits  for Executives,  Resolution  No. 2022-
54-CC.  In order to proceed  with  amending  the City's  contract  with  CalPERS  for cost sharing,  CalPERS
requires  a Resolution  of Intention,  an election  of  employees  agreeing  to the  contract  change,  and
adoption  of an ordinance  amending  the City's  contract  with  CalPERS.  At its October  10, 2023 meeting,
City  Council  adopted  Resolution  No.  2023-69-CC  declaring  its intent  to amend  the  contract  with
CalPERS  to implement  a cost sharing  program.  Furthermore,  the Executives  conducted  a secret ballot
election  on October  11, 2023  and a majority  of the group  voted  in favor  of the proposed  cost sharing
program.  The final  step to amend the contract  is to adopt an ordinance  authorizing  an amendment  to the
contract  between  the City  and CalPERS.  Today's  meeting  is to waive  the reading  in full  and introduce
an ordinance  authorizing  an amendment  to the contract.  Staff will  then come back for final  adoption  of
the ordinance  at the November  28, 2023 City  Council  meeting.

SUBJECT:  RESOLUTION  DECLARING  A CONTINUED  EMERGENCY  AND
AUTHORIZING  REPAIR,  REPLACEMENT  OR MAINTENANCE  ACTIVITIES  OF
PUBLIC  FACILITIES  RELATED  TO THE URBAN ORCHARD,  CITY PROJECT  NO.
539-PRK  WITHOUT  PUBLIC  BIDDING,  PURSUANT  TO  THE  EMERGENCY
CONTRACTING  PROCEDURES  OF THE SOUTH GATE MUNICIPAL  CODE AND
THE CALIFORNIA  PUBLIC CONTRACT  CODE

PURPOSE:  To declare an emergency still exists and to authorize the repair, replacement  or
maintenance activities of public facilities related to the Urban Orchard Project without  public
bidding.  The Los Angeles County Department  of Public Health, Solid Waste  Division
("County")  issued a Corrective Action Order requiring construction to stop on the project. The
declaration of emergency is necessary to streamline the process  to procure  a replacement
contractor to provide maintenance activities to preserve the site in a safe condition until the
County authorizes construction work on the project to resume.

RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City Council will consider making a finding and adopting
a Resolution  declaring an emergency still exists and authorizing  repair, replacement or
maintenance activities of public facilities related to the Urban Orchard, City Project No. 539-
PRK, without public bidding, pursuant to the emergency contracting procedures of the South
Gate Municipal Code and the California Public Contract Code.

FISCAL IMPACT:  There is no impact to the General Fund. The Urban Orchard Project
("Project") has received a total of $30.5 million in grant and other funds for design, construction,
operations, and maintenance, as summarized below, inclusive of a $5,000,000 grant from
Caltrans.

ANALYSIS:  The Project was under construction and approximately 80% of construction work
has been completed. On December 29, 2022, the City received a Corrective Action Order
("Order") from the County. The Order required the City to stop all construction activities  until
such a time as a Post Closure Land Use Plan ("PCLUP")  for the Project site was approved by the
County. Given the PCLUP approval process and input received to date, it will take at least
several months, possibly six or more, to obtain approval.

  1
  24
 To  avoid  the  significant  delay  damages  that  would  be payable  by  the  City  to the  general
contractor  during  a prolonged  suspension  of the project  pending  approval  of the PCLUP,  the City
Council  terminated  the general  contractor's  agreement  at a Special  City  Council  meeting  on
February  6, 2023.  Such termination  provided  both  immediate  and long-term  cost savings  to the
City  but also created  an immediate  need for the City  to retain  an interim  contractor  to perform
certain  ongoing  maintenance  and safety  activities;  a need which  must  be met  sooner  than  the
time necessary  to engage in normal  public  bidding  procedures

The proposed  Resolution  declares  a continued  emergency  exists pursuant  to the authority  granted
by South  Gate Municipal  Code  § 1.54.470  and California  Public  Contract  Code  § 22050.  Those
Code  Sections  allow  cities,  by resolution,  to approve  the  City's  entry  into  contracts  without
engaging  in public  bidding  where  certain  emergency  conditions  are found  to have occurred.  Staff
continues  to believe  that the County's  Order  directing  all construction  work  to be ceased on the
Project,  constitutes  such an emergency  due to the public's  safety  with  an unfinished  construction
site and the need to respond  accordingly  to additional  directives  given  by the County  related  to
ensuring  public  safety.  Staff  is  recornrnending  that  the  City  Council  adopt  the  proposed
Resolution  so that the City  can avail  itself  of the accelerated  contracting  procedures  authorized
by those  Code  Sections.  The  Resolution,  (1)  declares  an emergency,  (2)  authorizes  the  City
Manager  to  take  such  actions  deemed  necessary  to  cause  the  maintenance  activities  to  be
performed  and to procure  the necessary  equipment,  services,  and supplies  all without  giving
notice  for bids for contracts,  (3) requires  that at each regularly  scheduled  City  Council  Meeting,
the  City  Manager  present  to the  Council  the reasons  justifying  why  the emergency  will  not
permit  a delay  resulting  from  a competitive  solicitation  for bids,  why  that action  is necessary  to
respond  to the emergency,  and that the City  Council  review  the emergency  action  to determine,
by a four-fifth's  vote, that there is a need to continue  the emergency  action  until  the emergency
action  is terminated.

The  City  is working  diligently  to secure  the PCLUP  approval.  The process  has been initiated
with  the  submittal  of technical  documents  such  as the Workplan  for  interim  measures  and a
Surnrnary  of Site Investigation,  and the City  continues  to address  the requirements  imposed  by
the County.

Since  the original  Resolution  declaring  an emergency  was  approved  by the  City  Council  on
February  6, 2023,  the following  contracts,  expenditures,  and milestones  have been undertaken:

  1,  NR Development  Inc., was informed  that Contract  No. 2021-66-CC  was terminated  by
  the City  Council  effective  February  13, 2023,  except  for maintenance  activities.  Staff
  met with  NR Development  Inc.,  to discuss  the steps to close out construction  activities
  and continue  maintenance  activities.  As of February  16, 2023, NR Development  Inc., is
  no longer  providing  any project  services  or maintenance  activities.

  2.  City  forces  are providing  maintenance  services  of the site. The site has been secured
  with  perimeter  fencing  and security  contract  services.

  3.  Coordination  with  the  Trust  for  Public  Land  ("TPL")  to  complete  the  process  to
  prepare  the technical  documents  necessary  to  secure  a replacement  contractor  was
  completed.  Preliminarily  selected  a recommended  interim  contractor;  conducted  a field
  review;  and  received  a fee proposal  for  the  interim  maintenance  and  construction

  25
   activities approved by the Local Enforcement Agency  ("LEA").  Received a proposal
  from the contractor and have begun negotiations.

  4.  Submitted to the LEA the Summary of Investigations Report, Workplan of Interim
  Control Measures ("WICM"),  Supplemental WICM and Phase II Workplan. Received
  approval of the WICM and conditional approval of the Phase II Workplan. Submitted  a
  revised WICM as requested by the LEA. Submitted the revised Phase II Workplan  on
  April 18, 2023. On May 9, 2023, the LEA approved the Revised WICM for which the
  safety measures were implemented  by May 12, 2023. To date three months  of

  5.  Approved a funding increase for TPL in the amount of $50,000. On January 24, 2023,
  the City Council approved a $250,000 budget for Amendment No. 6 to Contract No.

  budget increase of $50,000 was administratively  approved to align the amount of the

  the LEA.

  6.  A bid was received from LA Engineering to complete the construction of maintenance

  7.  Construction work has begun on the scope of work approved in the WICM. Progress to

  completing the north wetland slope stabilization and substantially completing backfill
  of the reservoir and stockpile management. Construction work has begun adjacent to
  the Bandini Channel. Pending work includes completion of the electrical distribution
  system, construction of the easement road, installation of the security cameras,  and
  boarding up of the education building, The work is scheduled to be completed  in
  December  2023.

  8.  Methane gas monitoring has begun, and five months of sampling has been completed.
  The final monitoring testing will be conducted in November. The completed sampling
  results are scheduled to be submitted to the LEA in December 2023. There are 16
  probes throughout the 7-acre site. One probe has detected traces of methane, however,
  the amount is below regulatory requirements.

BACKGROUND:  The Project is a part of the FY 2022/23 Capital Improvement Program. The
Project is located between the Los Angeles River, Firestone Boulevard, the Thunderbird Villa
Mobile Home Park, and the I-710 Freeway. Two primary purposes of the Project are to divert
and treat storm water run-off from the Los Angeles River and provide recreation opportunities to
South  Gate residents.

The Project is being constructed on a property that was used as an unpermitted landfill until 1949
by an entity laiown as Southeastern Disposal and By-Products. The property site is identified  in
CalRecycle's Solid Waste Information System ("SWIS") as an Unpermitted Closed Solid Waste

  3
  26
 Disposal  Site and SWIS  No. 19-AA-5545.  In 1984,  the State of California  Department  of Health
Services,  Toxic  Substances  Control  Division  concluded  that  the  clean-up  work  completed
effectively  mitigated  waste  constituents  to  proceed  with  the  Lewis  Homes  residential
development  project.  The requirements  of the PCLUP  came  into  effect  in 1988.  As  such,  the
project  site is subject  to State solid  waste regulations  that require  the PCLUP  before  any change
to the current  land use, construction,  or land preparation  can occur.

The Los Angeles  County  Department  of Public  Health,  Solid  Waste  Management  Program,  acts
as the  LEA  for  the  State  of  California's  Department  of Resources  Recycling  and Recovery
("CalRecycle").  The  County  is  authorized  by  Division  30  of  the  Public  Resources  Code
("PRC"),  Section  43209  and 45000,  Title  14 and 27 of the California  Code  of Regulations  (14
CCR  & 27 CCR),  to enforce  applicable  solid  waste  regulations  and to ensure  solid  waste  sites
meet  the  state  minimum  standards  within  the  County  of Los  Angeles.  As  such,  the  City  is
working  with  the LEA  to obtain  approval  of the PCLUP.

Construction  is  currently  at  the  80%  completion  stage.  Improvements  that  have  been
substantially  completed  include,  but are not limited  to, rough  grading,  drop inlet  for storm  water
diversion  structures  in the Bandini  Channel,  a wetland  overlook  area, the stream  adjacent  to the
education/flexible  space  building  and  wetland,  south  bio  swale,  construction  of  18  raised
planters,  planting  of  75  trees,  installation  of  the  prefabricated  education  center  and  the
restroorn/maintenance  building,  two  shade  structures,  a water  element  at  the  playground,
installation  of multi-use  walking  and bicycle  pathways,  exercise  equipment  located  at various
stages along the walking  and bicycle  paths, benches,  picnic  tables,  drinking  fountains,  trash cans,
and pathway  lighting.  The total estimated cost of improvements  completed  to date is over  $12
million.

The Project  has received  the listed  grants.  The process  has begun  to enter into an agreement  with
Caltrans  to receive  an additional  $5 million  for a grand total of $30.5 million.

Department  establishing  that  the  City  does  not  have  sufficient  manpower  to  perform  the
Maintenance  Activities  with  its own  forces,  and that the immediate  need for the performance  of

  DIRECTOR  OF  FINANCE  IN  THE  ADMINISTRATIVE  SERVICES  DEPARTMENT,
  THE  CORRESPONDING  JOB  CLASSIFICATION  SPECIFICATION,  AND  TO  DIRECT
  ST AFF  TO UPDATE  THE  TITLE  TO  THE  CONSOLIDATED  SALARY  PAY  TABLE

  PURPOSE:  To  retitle  the  Deputy  Director  of  Administrative  Services/Finance  to  Deputy
  Director  of Finance  in the Administrative  Services  Department,  and to update  the corresponding
  job classification  specifications  and salary pay table.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTION:  The City  Council  will  consider  adopting  a Resolution  amending
  Resolution  No. 6454 (Salary  Resolution  and Position  Classification  Plan) by taking  the following
  actions:
  l)  Retitle  the Deputy  Director  of Administrative  Services/Finance  to Deputy  Director  of
  Finance;  and
  2)  Approve  the update  to the job classification  specification,  direct  staff to update  the title on
  the consolidated  salary  pay  table,  and approve  the salary  pay table  to be updated  and
  returned  to the City  Council  for approval  on a semi-annual  basis each April  and October.

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  Approving  the retitling  of the job  classification  from  Deputy  Director  of
  Administrative  Services/Finance  to Deputy  Director  of Finance  and updating  the job classification
  specifications  will  have no fiscal  impact  to the Fiscal  Year 2023/24  Adopted  Budget.

  ANALYSIS:  For  the Fiscal  Year  2022/2023  Budget  Year,  the City  Council  authorized  the
  formation  of the Department  of Human  Resources,  which  previously  was a division  under  the
  Department  of Administrative  Services  and headed  by the Deputy  Director  of Administrative
  Services/Human  Resources  & Risk  Management.  On May  9, 2023,  as a result  of the creation  of
  the Department  of Human  Resources,  the  City  Council  approved  the retitling  of the Deputy
  Director  of Administrative  Services/Human  Resources  & Risk Management  to Deputy  Director  of
  Human  Resources,  which  better  describes  the duties  of the position.

  I

  31
 The  Administrative  Services  Department  is responsible  for handling  all  aspects  of the City's
finances  including  accounting,  accounts  payable,  accounts  receivable,  purchasing,  payroll,
investments,  utility  billing,  business  licensing,  budgeting,  and managing  the City's  inforination
technology  needs.  The Administrative  Services  Department  is comprised  of six divisions  over
which  the  Director  of  Administrative  Services  is  responsible:  Administration/Accounting,
Purchasing,  Business  License,  Customer  Service,  Information  Technology,  and Capital  Equipment
Asset Replacement.  While  the Director  of Administrative  Services  oversees  all these divisions  and
activities,  the Deputy  Director  of Administrative  Services/Finance's  area of responsibility  is
isolated  to plaru'iing,  directing,  overseeing,  and evaluating  the City's  financial  activities.  In an
effort  to more appropriately  title this position,  approval  is requested  to change the title from Deputy
Director  of Administrative  Services/Finance  to Deputy  Director  of Finance.

On October  23, 2023, the City's  previous  Deputy  Director  of Administrative  Services/Finance  was
promoted  to the position  of Director  of Administrative  Services  and the City  is now  in need to
recruit  for her replacement.  By titling  the position  appropriately  to Deputy  Director  of Finance,
the City  will  be able to attract  and recruit  viable  candidates  to assume the duties  needed.

The proposed  salary range for the Deputy  Director  of Finance  is based upon the same salary range
of the  existing  Deputy  Director  of Administrative  Services/Finance,  which  the  City  Council
approved  as part of the Fiscal  Year 2023/24  Adopted  Budget.

The proposed  job  classification  specification  is attached  reflecting  the change  of title  to Deputy
Director  of Finance  and staff  seeks direction  from  the City  Council  to update  the consolidated
salary  schedule.  On September  12, 2023,  City  Council  approved  Resolution  No. 2023-62-CC  to
adopt  a comprehensive  pay schedule  for all full-time,  part-time,  and elected  officials  to comply
with  California  Code of Regulations  Fq570.5  of the Public  Employees'  Retirement  Law  (PERL).
Prior  to the adoption  of the comprehensive  salary  schedule,  the employees'  pay  tables  were
maintained  on separate,  bargaining  unit specific  salary  schedules.

The  comprehensive  salary  schedule  consolidates  the  employees'  salaries  and wages  on one
document,  is easy to use, and immediately  reflects  the approved  changes  as authorized  by City
Council.  The comprehensive  salary  schedule  does create issues when  there multiple  items  are on
an agenda seeking  approval  to make changes  to job classification  specification  and/or  pay, each of
which  traditionally  has had the salary  schedule  attached  as an exhibit.  If City  Council  decides  to
pass all but one of the proposed  items  on the agenda  or continue  an item  and each item has the
same comprehensive  salary  schedule  attached,  City  Council  would  inadvertently  approve  the item
it decided  to deny or continue.  For example,  assume  an agenda  as one item  seeking  approval  to
create  a new  position,  another  agenda  items  seeking  approval  to update  an existing  position's
compensation,  and a third  agenda  item  reclassifying  a position  and adjusting  the salary  of the
position  and City  Council  decides  to continue  the last item but approve  the first two,  City  Council
would  inadvertently  have  approved  the reclassified  position's  title  and salary  because  it would
necessarily  have to appear on the comprehensive  salary  schedules  attached  to the first two items.

With  City Council  directing  staff on each passed item to update the comprehensive  salary schedule
instead  of approving  an attachment,  the dilemma  of inadvertent  approval  of an item  denied  or
continued  is eliminated  entirely.  While  the PERL  requires  the salary  schedule  be approved  and

  2

  32
 adopted  by City  Council  in accordance  with  the requirements  of applicable  public  meeting  laws,
it does not require  that every minor  adjustment  to the salary schedule  be effectuated  in this manner.
In fact,  the generally  accepted  practice  is to administratively  update  the salary  schedule  at the
direction  of City  Council,  post that change on the City's  website  to ensure consistent  and constant
transparency,  and bring  the comprehensive  salaiy  schedule  to City  Council  for official  approval
and adoption  on an annual  basis.  However,  in  an effort  to maintain  transparency,  Human
Resources  will  bring  the comprehensive  salary  schedule  to City  Councn  for  approval  and
adoption  on a semi-annual  basis during  the second  regular  City  Council  meeting  each April
and October.

BACKGROUND:  The City  must,  from  time to time,  add, remove,  reclassi'fy,  retitle,  update  or
otherwise  adjust  job  classifications,  job  specifications  and/or  compensation  in  the  Salary
Resolution  and Position  Classification  Plan in order to satisfy  the changing  needs and demands  of
the  City's  workforce.  In  response  to these  changing  needs  and  demands,  job  classification
specifications  must be amended  to more  closely  match  the tasks which  need to be performed  by
employees  in the City's  various  departments.

Human  Resources  staff  corresponded  with  the Division  Management  Association  (DMA)  Board
Members  to inform  them  of the retitled  classification,  and they  agree  with  the updated  job
classification  specification.

Code  Enforcement  Services
Code  enforcement  services  are  among  the  most  complex  and  challenging
services  that  government  agencies  provide.  According  to nationwide  studies,
property  values,  crime  rates,  insurance  rates,  business  development,  and the
sense  of  community  pride  can  be  directly  impacted  by the  successes  of  a
jurisdiction's  code  enforcement  program.

To aid jurisdictions  with  the difficult  task of maintaining  the quality  oflife  for its
citizens  through  such  programs,  Willdan  has assembled  a quality  staff  with
extensive  public  agency  experience  in the areas of neighborhood  preservation,
housing  inspection,  and  code  enforcement.  Our  expertise  includes  the
development  and  implementation  of inspection  programs  designed  to ensure
public  safety,  promote  community  involvement,  and protect  the  quality-of-life
issues through  community  education  and enforcement  of municipal  and related
codes  including  preparation  for, and participation  in, prosecution  by city and district  attorneys.

Scope of Work

Code  Enforcement  Services
Code  enforcement  services  are  among  the  most  complex  and  challenging
services  that  government  agencies  provide.  According  to nationwide  studies,
property  values,  crime  rates,  insurance  rates,  business  development,  and the
sense  of community  pride  can  be directly  impacted  by the  successes  of a
jurisdiction's  code enforcement  program.

To aid jurisdictions  with  the difficult  task of maintaining  the quality  of life for its
citizens  through  such  programs,  Willdan  has assembled  a quality  staff  with
extensive  public  agency  experience  in the areas of neighborhood  preservation,
housing  inspection,  and  code  enforcement.  Our  expertise  includes  the
development  and implementation  of inspection  programs  designed  to ensure
public  safety,  promote  community  involvement,  and protect  the quality-of-life
issues through  community  education  and enforcement  of municipal  and related
codes including  preparation  for, and participation  in, prosecution  by city and district  attorneys.

Willdan  provides  the following  Code Enforcement  Services:

  *  Inspection  services  for HUD section  8 programs.

  *  Review,  study,  and analysis  of existing  programs.

  Development  of ordinances  and writing  of grant  proposals.

  *  Neighborhood  cleanup  and improvement  programs.

  *  Community  education  programs.

  *  Development  of educational  materials.

  *  Provide project managers and/or supervisors as onsite "employees."
  *  Provide full-time, part-time, interim, and/or weekend staff as onsite "employees."
  *  Vehicle  abatement  and parking  enforcement.

  *  ASSiSt in enforcement,  including  preparation  and participation  in prosecution  by city and
  district  attorneys.

  *  Illegal street/food  vendor  enforcement.

  *  The registration  and enforcement  of vacation  rentals.

  *  The regulation  of group  and/or  sober  living  homes.

  h  Inspection,  regulation,  and enforcement  of marijuana  dispensaries  and grow  houses.

  SUBJECT:  AGREEMENT  WITH  DESIGN  WEST  ENGINEERING  FOR
  ENGINEERING  DESIGN  SERVICES  FOR  THE  EMERGENCY  BACK-UP
  GENERATOR  REPLACEMENT  PROJECT,  CITY  PROJECT  N0. 704-GEN

  PURPOSE: To award a professional services agreement to Design West Engineering to prepare
  design and construction documents for the Emergency Back-Up Generator Replacement Project,
  City Project No. 704-GEN ("Project").

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider:
  a.  Approving an Agreement with Design West Engineering for engineering  design services
  for the Emergency Back-Up Generator Replacement Project, City Project No. 704-GEN,
  in an amount not to exceed $178,665;
  b.  Authorizing the City Manager to approve contingency amendments to the proposed
  Agreement at a cumulative cost of up to $50,000; and
  c.  Authorizing the Mayor to execute the Agreement in a form acceptable to the City
  Attorney.

  FISCAL IMPACT:  There is no fiscal impact to the General Fund. The proposed Agreement is
  in the amount of $178,665 and it will be funded by America Rescue Plan Act ("ARPA")  funds
  budgeted in the FY 2022/23 Capital Improvement Program. A summary  of budgeted funds and
  proposed expenditures  is shown below:

  Budget  Amount
  Agreement  Professional  Design Services  $178,665
  De-sign  Contingencies  -  $50,000
  Pro,je-ct Manage-ment and Staff Time  $25,000
  Total  -Proposed  Expenditures  $253,665

  ANALYSIS:  The City of South Gate has a number of critical facilities that need to be
  operational during periods of public emergencies such as severe storms or earthquakes. These
  facilities house functions that are necessary for the provision  of public services  such as
  government operations, public safety, critical infrastructure services, emergency  response  and

  I

  99
 housing  of displaced  residents.  In order  for these facilities  to function  during  all emergencies,  it
is necessary  to have  in place  adequate  and reliable  emergency  back-up  generators  capable  of
supplying  power  to the facilities  during  power  outages.  The  following  five  (5)  City  facilities
have been identified  as critical  facilities  for this purpose:  City  Hall,  the Police  Station,  the old
courthouse  building,  the Public  Works  Corporate  Yard  ("City  Yard")  and the South  Gate Park
Municipal  Auditorium  recently  renamed  the  Henry  C.  Gonzalez  Municipal  Auditorium
("Municipal  Auditorium").

The City  Hall  building  is the center  of South Gate city governance.  In the event of an emergency,
it is important  that staff be available  to oversee  emergency  operations  and the City  Council  have
an operating  venue  in which  to hold  emergency  meetings  when  necessary  to provide  direction  to
City  staff,  authorize  necessary  expenditures,  and approve  emergency  resolutions  as required.  The
Police  Station  is  a 24-hour  operation  that  is  critical  to  public  safety,  especially  during
emergencies.  Maintaining  power  at the  Police  Station  is  critical  in  order  to  provide  for
emergency  communications  and  dispatch,  among  other  things.  The  South  Gate  Courthouse
building  is currently  undergoing  redesign  for offices  for Human  Resources,  IT,  and the Police
Department  to also house  the City's  Emergency  Operations  Center  ("EOC").  The EOC  acts as a
focal  point  for communication  and coordination  of emergency  services  during  disasters  and other
emergencies  and, as such, it is of utmost  importance  to maintain  power  to the EOC  during  such
events.  The City  Yard  houses  all the field  operations  of the Public  Works  Department  including
controls  for the City's  water  system,  street,  building  and electrical  crews  that  are called  upon
during  emergencies  to  address  infrastructure-related  public  safety  issues.  To  provide  this
function,  power  is required.  Finally,  the Municipal  Auditorium  is designated  as both  a cooling
center  during  severe  heat waves  and as emergency  housing  for residents  that are displaced  by a
disaster  or  other  emergency  impacting  the  community.  To  serve  these  purposes  during  an
emergency,  it is necessary  for the Municipal  Auditorium  to have reliable  back-up  power  in the
event of a power  failure.

Four  of these facilities  currently  have back-up  generators  that are in need of replacement.  The
back-up  generators  are all over 20 years old and some are close to 40 years old.  Due to their  age,
the generators  are less reliable,  prone  to have maintenance  issues and they are nearing  the end of
their  serviceable  life.  In addition,  the existing  generators  at City  Hall,  Police  Station,  City  Yard,
and  the  Municipal  Auditorium  do  not  have  the  capacity  to  permit  full  operations  to  be
maintained  during  emergency  situations.  For example,  the City  Hall  generator  only  provides  for
emergency  standby  lighting  and just  enough  power  for the Information  Technology  ("IT")  server
room.  The  current  generator  cannot  support  all the electrical  demands  normally  required  on a
workday  by staff  located  at the City  Hall  .  All  the generators  are similarly  undersized  for the
power  needs  of  the  facilities  they  are designated  to  in  order  to  ensure  the  continuance  of
governance  during  such  emergency  situations.  As  a result,  the  ability  of these  buildings  to
operate  as needed  during  emergencies  is very limited.

The  Emergency  Back-Up  Generator  Replacement  Project  will  replace  these  four  back-up
generators  with  new  generators  that are designed  to meet 'full building  operational  needs taking
into  account  today's  electrical  demands,  as well  as, any future  increases  in demand  that can be
identified  at this time  and for a length  of time  of at least 5-days  before  needing  to be refueled.  In
addition,  the  project  will  provide  a generator  for  the  Courthouse  building  which  is being

  2

  100
 redesigned to house City offices and the EOC. The Courthouse building  does not currently  have
an emergency  generator.

BACKGROUND:  The Emergency Back-Up Generator Replacement Project is in the FY
2023/24 Capital Improvement Program.  It is budgeted in the amount of $1.75 million, with
ARPA Funds.  The project entails replacing the existing back-up generators at facilities
mentioned above, and providing service to the South Gate Courthouse which is scheduled to be
operational within the next two to three years. An agreement is needed to begin the design
phase.

The proposed Agreement was procured through a competitive process in which an RFP was
published on the City website and in trade journals. On September 20, 2023, the City received
five proposals which are listed below.

  Consultant  Fee Proposal
  1.  Design  West  Engineering  $178,6-65
  2.  EDA, Inc.  $49,900
  3.  Borrelli  and Associates  $438,000
  4.  P2S Engineering  $465,725
  5.  s.y.  Lee Associates  $1,031,176

A selection committee evaluated the proposals. The selection committee consisted of Harvey
Gobas and Charles Herbertson, both Project Managers for Willdan Engineers, and Lorenzo
Camargo, Acting Associate Engineer for the City of South Gate. The review criteria weighed  a
number of factors including project understanding, consultant project team qualifications  and
experience on similar projects, project work plan and schedule, and demonstrated technical
ability  of the firm  and project  team.

Design West Engineering  received the overall highest ranking from the panel (taking  into
account the evaluation criteria) and is therefore recommended for the contract.

Design West Engineering is located in the City of San Bernardino, California.  They have been
providing mechanical, electrical, and plumbing ("MEP") engineering design services for over 23
years and have been providing services to South Gate for over 10 years. The project manager
assigned to the project has over 24 years of experience in MEP design and is the Electrical
Department Head for Design West Engineering.  He will be supported in the design effort by a
Senior Electrical  Project Manager with 12 years of experience who has a professional
engineering license in electrical engineering.  Design West Engineering submitted the best
overall proposal, has worked on several similar emergency  generator projects, and clearly
demonstrated in their proposal the expertise needed to provide the services requested.

The proposed agreement is in the amount of $178,665. The fee is reasonable and competitive
and within the expected cost range for this project. EDA provided a fee proposal in the amount
of $49,900. However, it was the consensus of the proposal review team that their proposal failed
to demonstrate the necessary experience and expertise for this project.  As such, the team
believes EDA's proposed fee may be the result of underestimating the project requirements and

 scope.

The  services  in  the  proposed  agreement  include  project  management;  utility  coordination;
evaluation  of existing  back-up  emergency  generators;  evaluation  of power  demand  requirements
at the  various  facilities;  development  of probable  cost  estimates  for  planning  purposes  and
engineering  design;  development  of plans,  specifications,  detailed  estimates  and bid documents;
construction  bidding  and support;  and project  record  as-builts  plans and closeout.

Design  for this project  is scheduled  to begin in November  2023 and conclude  in September  2023.

PROJECT UNDERSTANDING
Design West Engineering will provide engineering services for the City of South Gate"s initiative to upgrade
the emergency backup power systems at five essential city facilities. This crucial project aims to ensure the
continuity of critical services during power blackouts and other events that could result in long-term power
outages. The five facilities under consideration are:

  1. City of South  Gate  Police  Department
  2. City of South  Gate  City Hall
  3. Public  Works  Maintenance  Yard
  4. South  Gate  Park Auditorium
  5. Court  House  Building

APPROACH
Phase I I Assessment
Task 1: Project Management  l In the initial phase of the project, Design West Engineering will appoint our
Electrical Department Head Roy Morales as the Project Manager to oversee all project activities and ensure
effective coordination with relevant stakeholders. He will maintain continuous communication with the City
Project Manager and other stakeholders, facilitating meetings for the assessment of each facility's existing
backup power system. These meetings will involve communicating conceptual layouts for facility modifications
and coordinating with City officials, utility companies, and regulatory agencies. Additionally, monthly project
status reports will be provided to keep all parties informed of progress.

  117
   Pige  I

Task 2: Assessment of Existing Backup Systems l The next step involves assessing the performance and
condition of existing backup systems at all five facilities. Ourteam will document electrical system configurations,
MEP layouts, and any major deficiencies. We will conduct interviews with building maintenance staff, review
maintenance records, and document power platform and electrical distribution layouts.

Task 3: Power Needs Assessment l Subsequently, we will review the inventory of equipment relying on
electrical power at all five facilities and interview City staff to determine current and future power demands.
This will allow us to establish backup power requirements for each facility and develop probable cost estimates
for each scenario, ensuring a comprehensive understanding  of the project scope.

Phase 2 I Design & Specification  Development
Task4: RegulatoryReviewand  Permittingl  Duringthis phase, Design West Engineeringwill ensure compliance
with State and local building codes, air emission standards, and other relevant regulations at all five facilities.
We will obtain all required plan checks, reviews, and permits, while also coordinating with City officials,
utility managers, and relevant agencies. Additionally, we will document any required safety equipment  and
operational  procedures  to meet  legal standards.

Task 5: Conceptual Plans l Conceptual plans will be developed with recommended revisions to building
 ayouts for all five facilities. This will include accommodat'ng generator platform revisions if needed, external
equipment for emergency power connection, outlining MEP modifications, and providing planning-level cost
estimates  for each  facility.

Task 6: Equipment and Backup Generator Specifications  l To ensure optimal equipment selection, we
will develop specifications for backup power generators and related equipment at all five facilities. This wi
encompass recommending operating procedures, maintenance requirements, warranty specifications,  and
manufacturers. Equipment specifications will be closely coordinated with building and platform layouts, with
the inclusion of Transfer Switch options as needed.

Task 7: Plans and Specifications for Installation  l Detailed plans and specifications for building and MEP
modifications, generatorinstallation, and building enclosures will be developed for all five facilities. These plans
will include instructions for the removal and salvage of old equipment. We will submit 60% and 90% design
plans for City review, ensuring alignment with project objectives, and prepare final plans and specificat'ons
signed by licensed engineers. Coordination with sub-consultants, utilities, and stakeholders will be a priority.

Phase 3 I Construction
Task 8: Cost Estimates l In the construct'on phase, Design West Engineering will bring on HLCM as a sub-
consultant who will then develop 50% and 100% detailed cost estimates for backup power generator
procurement and installation at each of the f've facilities. These cost estimates will break down expenses for
hardware, electronic options, building modifications, platform changes, and MEP modifications, supported  by
documentation  from  recent  similar  bids.

Task 9: Construction Bidding Phase l Our team will prepare a Construction Bid Package for all five facilities,
attend pre-bid meetings, assist in analyzing bids, and manage quest'ons and responses to bidders. Addenda
will be prepared as needed to ensure clarity and transparency throughout the bidding process.

Task 10: Pre-construchon  Meeting and Job Site Meetings I Additionally, Design West Engineering will actively
participate in pre-construction and job site meetings as necessary for all five facilities, preparing agendas and
meeting  minutes  to facilitate  effective  communicat'on.

Task11: Respond to Requests for Information and Submittals I Throughout the construction  phase, Design
West Engineering will respond to contractor's requests forinformat'on, provide field design recommendations,
and maintain a log of RFI responses and meetings, ensuring that the project proceeds smoothly and according
topan.

This comprehensive  approach will enable Design West Engineering to assess, design, and upgrade the
emergency backup generators at all five essential City of South Gate facilities, ensuring their reliability during
power outages and emergencies.

  SUBJECT:  PURCHASE  ORDER  FOR  RENEWAL  OF  MAINTENANCE  AND
  SUPPORT  SERVICES  SOFTWARE  WITH  PULSIAM  FOR  THE  POLICE
  DEPARTMENT

  PURPOSE:  To  renew  the  existing  agreement  with  Pulsiam  for  maintenance  and  support
  services  which  includes  Computer  Aided  Dispatch  ("CAD")  and Records  Management  Systems
  ("RMS")  for the Police  Department.  The  South  Gate Municipal  Code  requires  that all agreements
  more  than $50,000  be approved  by the City  Council;  therefore,  the purchase  order  agreement  needs
  to go before  the Council  for renewal.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTION:  The  City  Council  will  consider  authorizing  the  issuance  of  a
  purchase  order  agreement  with  Pulsiam  to renew  the maintenance  and support  services  software
  for Fiscal  Year  2023/2024  for the Police  Department  in the amount  of  $119,320.33.

  FISCALIMPACT:  Funds  for  these  services  were  included  in  the  Fiscal  Year  2023/24
  Municipal  Budget.

  ANALYSIS:  This  purchase  order  is for the renewal  of an existing  sole source  proprietary  software
  agreement  that does not require  bidding  and complies  with  City  purchasing  guidelines.

  BACKGROUND:  For the past  30 years,  the Police  Department  has contracted  with  Pulsiam  to
  provide  24-hour  support  for  its  CAD  and RMS  systems.  The  CAD  and  RMS  systems  are the
  foundation  of information  technology  that  enables  the Police  Department  to receive  9-1-1  calls  in
  the dispatch  center  and generate  calls  for  service  that  are sent electronically  to police  officers  in
  the  field.  The  system  is  also  an  integrated  database  for  the  processing  and  storage  of  law
  enforcement  information,  including  crime  and arrest  reports.

  CAD  and RMS  are an integrated  system  designed  specifically  for law  enforcement  operations.
  CAD  is a real-time  system,  which  automatically  verifies  addresses,  tracks  and manages  incoming
  calls,  prioritizes  calls  for service,  and tracks  on-duty  personnel  activity.  RMS  provides  reporting
  and analytical  capabilities  for investigations  and generates  statistics  for the Uniform  Crime  Report
  to the state and the federal  governments.  Mobile  Data  and e-Reporting  modules  allow  officers  to

 access  dispatch information  in the field,  provide access to our secure  law  enforcement  network,

complex software system is necessary to keep up with modifications, technology issues, changes
in existing laws, and other constantly evolving mandates to law enforcement.

  Overview  of how water gets from our wells to the customer.
  The City has eight active wells that pump from the groundwater  aquifer  approximately  2.7 billion
  gallons annually,  or 8,300 Acre Feet (AF).  The water is directly  pumped  to the water distribution
  system or to six (6) reservoirs  which  hold and allow  the Water  Division  to regulate  the flow  of
  water during  low and high demand periods throughout  the City service area. Approximately  90%
  of the City  is served by our Water  Division,  with  the remaining  community  sections  served by
  private  water companies.  For those served by the City, the water travels through  approximately
  135 miles of underground  pipes to the 14,300 customers  served by us.

  That water is delivered  to each customer  through  a service  line and water meter that have been

How does the City know how much a customer uses during any billir5;r cvde?
The water meters are used to measure water usage for every billing cycle. Each meter  has a set of
dials which displays a series of numbers called the register.  Figure 1 shows a typical register  for
a 3/4-inch water meter with the series of numbers.  The far-right number on the white dials, in this
case where the number five (5) shows, reflects a single hundred cubic feet ("HCF")  used by the
customer.  The next number reflects each 10 HCF increments, and the dial progresses  from  there.
A single HCF represents 748 gallons.  In Figure 1 the number reads 0845.91, which represents  that
almost 846 HCF of water or over 632,060 gallons have passed through  the meter since  it was
installed.  Water meters are read at the completion  of every billing  cycle. The usage for each cycle
for which a customer is billed is calculated by taking the difference between the current  meter  read
and the prior meter read number.  For example, the usage for this water meter would be 10 HCF if
the prior meter read was 0835.91.  The customer would then be billed for 10 HCF.

 The meters are read monthly  for evety water customer.  Each day Water Meter Readers go out to
read a portion  of the City which  includes  both residential  and commercial.  The City's  customers
are divided  into 8 read routes and two routes are read each day with approximately  1,000 customers
within  the two routes daily.  Two full-time  City employees  with a combined  23 years of service
accomplish  the task.  As a matter  of historical  practice,  each employee  within  the Public  Works
Water  Division  is trained  in how to read meters, whicli  provides  a substantial  back-up  process
should the need arise due to vacations,  illness, or training  absences.

There are two processes  for reading  meters.  Of the 14,300  meters, 2,334 are Automatic  Meter
Reading  ("AMR")  meters which  allow  the meter to be read from simply  walking  or driving  by.
The data is transmitted  automatically  from the water meter to the handheld  reading  device via a
transponder  attached to the meter.  For the remaining  11,966 meters, a Water Meter Reader must
physically  observe the register  and then manually  input the numbers  into their handheld  reading
device.  To read the dial, the Water Meter Reader must lift the lid of the box and then may need to
spray the register  dial face due to discoloration/dirt  or even clear the meter box of accumulated
debris.  Our handheld  devices  have an alert setting  that will  beep if a number  being inputted  is
25% higher or lower than the previous  consumption  number  billed  for the customer.  This alerts
the Water Meter  Reader to check the dial and the number  being inputted  again for accuracy.  If
verified,  the Meter Reader Water then replaces the lid and moves on to the next meter box.

At the end of the day, the handheld  devices are returned  to their docking  station where the device
downloads  the data collected  from  the day, is recharged,  and the next day route information  is
uploaded  onto the device.  The data from  the readings  are transmitted  to the Water  Customer
Service Division  in the Administrative  Services Department  for billing  purposes.

On the following  business day after the reading data is uploaded  to the billing  system, it is retrieved
by Customer  Service  Representatives  ("CSRs")  in the Water  Customer  Service Division;  this is
where the billing  process begins.  The CSR conducts  a second review  of the meter reads, which
helps detect potential  billing  enors.  One of the tools used during  this process is the Edit Listing
Report,  better described  as those meters exceeding  the 25% usage variance.  When a meter read
has a 25% increase or decrease in consumption,  the account will  be included  in this report.  This
prompts  the CSR to send a service request back to the Water Meter Reader for a second or third
read of that water  meter.  If a read is returned  as being  adjusted,  then the CSR will  make the
necessary adjustments  to the account to calculate  an accurate bill for our customer.  Once the meter
reads are confirmed  and finalized,  the CSR can continue  the billing  process.  Thereafter,  the CSRs
are also responsible  for managing  accounts  receivable,  creating,  and tracking  any additional
customer  service requests.  Customers  are encouraged  to review  their bills  and inquire  about the
accuracy  of their bill. The CSR can place a request for a meter to be reread. If it is determined  that
the bill went out in error, the CSR will request a billing  adjustment  to be applied to the customer's
account.

 Why can a customer's  usa5ze varv from month  to month?
There are a variety  of reasons consumption  can change from month  to month  or year to year.  Many
of these reasons  are often  not very  apparent  to the user.  First,  it is important  to understand  that
each water customer  has a unique  set of facts about their water usage and will  veiy unlikely  be like
their neighbor  or neighborhood.  Factors  such as:

  1.  Number  of individuals  living  in the house.  According  to the Pacific  Institute,  as of
  September  2022, the average  per capita usage in South Gate was 105 gallons  per day.  The
  number  of people  in a household  whether  peimanently  or temporarily  can increase  or
  decrease  a month  over month  water bill.
  2.  The number  of billing  days in a billing  cycle varies  from  month  to month  due to the work
  schedule  and billing  calendar.  Usually,  December  is the shortest  billing  period  with  an

  average  of only 23 days.  January  is the longest  billing  period  with  the read averaging  about
  39 days.  Thus, the month  over month  increase  could  potentially  be as much as 40%.
  3.  Landscape  watering  can impact  the billing.  The impact  can vary  even more  for urban
  versus  suburban  and rural  areas.  The  Public  Policy  Instihite  of California  estimates,
  depending  on where  the customer  lives (urban,  suburban,  or rural),  their outdoor  usage can
  account  for up to 40% of their  daily  usage in the warmer  months.
  4.  Whether  a  household  has  water  efficient  appliances  ranging  from  showerheads,
  dishwashers,  washing  machines  to toilets.  For example,  toilets  manufactured  prior  to 1996,
  on average,  use between  5 to 7 gallons  per flush.  Since  about  2014,  toilets  have  been
  manufactured  to use about 1.6 gallons.  Newer  appliances  have been manufactured  to use
  up to 40% less water  over the last 15 years.
  5.  The Institute  of Agriculture  & Natural  Resources  reports  that warmer  months  have  an
  impact  on water  usage.  During  the warm  summer  months  and the growing  season, water
  use tends to increase  as we try to help meet the water demands  of lawns,  vegetable  gardens,
  flowers,andtrees.  However,ourwateruseinsidethehousecanalsotendtoincreaseduring
  the summer  months;  something  we may not always  realize.  We may create more laundry,
  take more frequent  showers,  and teenagers  may be home during  the day instead of at school
  and using  more water.
  6.  Whether  a household  has a pool.  According  to many  studies  cited  by industry  experts,
  water evaporation  rates vary based on water temperature,  air temperature,  wind  speed, wind
  volatility,  sun exposure,  and humidity  levels.  The average  pool  water  evaporation  rate is
  about a quarter  of an inch of water  per day or more than two inches  in a week,  which  on a
  33' x 18' swirnrning  pool (an average  pool size) is more than 2,500  liters  or approximately
  600 gallons  a week;  this may vary depending  on your  climate  and the factors  listed  above.
  7.  Water  so:tteners  use water  to operate.  Water  Softeners  nortnally  have a reserve  capacity  of
  20 to 25% before  it regenerates;  this means that it regenerates  when the resin beads are 75

 Why the increase  in rereads and billinz  adiustments?
There  are multiple  reasons  for this increase.  Starting  with  one of the more common  reasons  being
human  error.  The meter  read collected  may have been unclear  due to severe discoloration  of the
register  dial cover  or debris  on the meter  box which  may have prevented  a clear reading.  While
not intentional,  the Water  Meter  Reader  has forced  a number  into the device.

Another  reason  is the meter  itself  may  be malfunctioning.  According  to the American  Water
Works  Association  (AWWA),  meters  are to have a 98.5 to 101.5  accurate  read.  Anything  outside
those thresholds  is considered  a faulty  meter.  The only way to determine  such is for Public  Works
to pull  the meter  and send it to a third-party  testing  lab.  Usually,  a faulty  meter  fails  to meet the
98.5 threshold  due to worn  parts or sediment  that has dislodged  and impacted  the spinner.  This
means an under read has occurred  and thus to the benefit  of the customer.  The new meter  installed
as a result  of the meter being pulled  for testing  will  pick up the more accurate  customer  usage read.

As a result  of this investigation,  we have found  some technological  issues.  The first  is that the
City  upgraded  its handheld  reading  devices  and software  at the beginning  of the calendar  year
(2023).  The devices  were  set to "Supervisor"  mode  rather  than "Operator"  mode.  Whether  this
impacted  the reads is impossible  to determine  with  confidence.  All  such devices  have now been
set to the proper  Operator  mode  for inputting  in the field.

We have also realized  that when the City replaced  and upgraded  the meter data collection  software
a year ago, we did not do an adequate job of passing  along the capabilities  of the new Itron  system
to staff  in terms  of reporting  and tracking.  For example,  it provides  the ability  to document  a
reread  with  photos  which  can be provided  to staff handling  water  billing  and to the customer,  if
requested.

In addition,  the control  settings  on the Edit Listing  Report  in the Eden financial  software  for usage
variance  may have been set in conflict  with  recommended  industry  standards  which  could  have
led to some water  consumption  alerts not being  communicated  by the handheld  device  in the field
and being  left off the Edit Listing  Report.  The issue is being  tested in the field  after resetting  the
alert limit  thresholds  within  the Eden system.

Finally,  there  may  be an increased  level  of customer  anxiety  due to the timing  with  the City
reimposing  shutoffs  due to nonpayment  of bills.  During  the COVID  pandemic,  the City  Council
directed  that water  service  not be shut off for nonpayment  as too many  households  were being
financially  impacted  due to layoffs.  Due to the closure  of businesses  and schools,  more  people
were  home  for  much  longer  periods  which  would  cause water  usage  to rise  significantly.  In
addition,  the state implemented  a new shutoff  process  in response  to the COVID  pandemic  which
prohibits  the shutoff  of any customer  for nonpayment  until  the account  is at least 60 days past due.
This state regulation  requires  us to issue a past due statement  and a past due letter being  sent to the
customer  mailing  address.  Also,  the staff  delivers  weekly  door hangers  that are placed  on the
customer's  door  in keeping  with  the directive  by the City  Council  of being  proactive  in helping

aware  of how  to address  matters,  handle  the processes  in the field  or at the customer  billing  counter,
and, most  importantly,  improving  communication  between  the field  and customer  billing  counter.

RECOMMENDATIONS:
During  this  exhaustive  investigation  and  interaction  with  our  customers,  several  elements  have
been identified  and are presented  for City  Council  consideration:

  1.  Most  importantly,  customer  service.  This  is  always  an  important  element  for  any
  organization  to be constantly  working  on.  Our  goal  should  always  be to emulate  how  we
  ourselves  would  wish  to be treated  and respected.  It is important  that we frequently  remind
  ourselves  that  every  contact  will  be seen  as the  face  of the  organization  and  how  our
  customers  will  be le:[t with  its impression.  Customer  service  can only  be improved  through
  better  communication.  We  have  begun  adopting  the  theme  of "See  something,  Say
  something."  This  is simply  because  we all have  an obligation  to alert the right  people  when
  we see or hear something  that is out of place  or extraordinary.  In this case, when  our CSRs
  begin  to see the volume  of rereads  increase  on the Edit  Listing  Report,  they  will  alert  their
  supervisor.  This  will  allow  us to investigate  trends  sooner.

  Customer  service  also goes to making  sure our customers  feel like  they  can approach  City
  Hall  and  be  heard.  In  recent  weeks,  we  have  added  training  such  as de-escalation
  interaction  and will  be looking  for  additional  training  programs  for persoru'iel  interacting
  with  the public  on a regular  basis.  The standard  is treating  others  as you  would  have them
  treat  you.  Even  when  that  customer  may  be aggressive  in their  words  and/or  tone,  it is our

  9

  168
   obligation  to remain  respectful  and listen to their story; this is a very simple  and to the point
  expectatxon.

2.  We propose  increasing  our public  education  of water programs.  This education  includes  a
  more  comprehensive  effort  in  posting  infomiation  on  the  website  and  social  media
  platforms  with  topics  on how to read your meter,  how can you identify  possible  leaks, and
  reminding  customers  of warming  weather  impacts  on usage.  A frequently  asked questions
  and answer  sheet will  also be developed,  as well  as, actively  promoting  (323)  563-9586  as

  a number  to call about bills  or email  at customerhelp(2Dsogate.org..

  Through  education,  we have the ability  to remind  customers  of the very generous  programs

  that may  be able to assist them  in paying  or staying  current  with  utility  bills.  This  has
  begun  by  our  effort  in bringing  the LBCA  into  City  Hall  on November  15th to assist
  residents  in determining  if they qualify  for assistance  by the State of California  and if so,
  approving  them for the program  that same day.  We also need to promote  continued  access
  to the ARPA  funds  the City  Council  has previously  allocated  to assist with  water  bills
  impacted  by COVID.

3.  Protocols  need to be developed.  One element  that clearly  has become  evident  is procedures
  have not been written  down  and new employees  have not been trained  on the systems  as
  completely  as they should  be. This can be something  as simple  as alerting  supervisors  when
  the meter  covers have become  too discolored  to be read clearly.  While  a meter replacement
  can cost approximately  $150,  if the dials cannot  be read reliably,  then it is time to replace
  the meter.

  In addition,  the upgrade  of the handheld  devices  has occurred,  and we did not thoroughly
  ask questions  from  the manufacturer  to be sure we were fully  trained  on mode  settings  and
  their  capability.  This  same  aspect  of technology  is to make  sure we  stay  current  on
  practices  and upgrades  that the manufacturer  provides  on their  software.  We have found
  that we are not using the latest upgrade  from  Itron  of their  software.

  We have already  begun  to use the photo  capture  program  when  a reread occurs.  This will
  allow  the Water  Customer  Service  Representatives  and/or  customers  to view  the picture  to
  make sure it matches  up with  the reread number  provided.

4.  Consider  establishing  an incentive  program  that can help residents  upgrade  to more water
  efficient  devices.  Metropolitan  Water  District  and  other  organizations  offered  such
  incentives  during  previous  drought  periods  to help customers  lower  water  consumption.
  Replacing  items  like  toilets,  showerheads,  dishwashers  and washing  machines  could
  potentially  help a resident  save thousands  of dollars  each year.

5.  Consider  a program  of meter  replacements  and upgrades  where  the data is transmitted  via
  the internet  and allows  customers  to view  their  data in real time.  Many  purveyors  have or
  are installing  such water meters  which  use technology,  software,  and antenna  systems  that

  10

  169
   the City  does not  currently  have.  While  such  upgraded  meters  can themselves  have
  misreads  due to the device  antenna becoming  compromised,  they reduce human  interaction
  and thus the possibility  of inputting  wrong  data.  More  importantly,  it begins  to enhance
  transparency  between  the City  and customer  and helps customers  track usage in real time.
  The customer  can set up aleits  and get reports  on their  usage that allow  them to be even
  better  stewards  of this precious  resource.

  In the meantime,  we are stepping  up our replacement  of meters  where  the register  dial
  cannot  be clearly  seen by the Water  Meter  Reader.  We don't  have a complete  account  of
  how many  of these, but we have already  purchased  about 150 AMR  meters with  the intent
  of placing them into service  this current  fiscal  year.  An AMR  meter  costs about  $275  a
  piece.

  6.  Workload  balance.  Public  Works  is also investigating  whether  the workload  balance  for
  Water  Meter  Readers  and daily  reads is consistent  with  industry  best practices  for manual
  reading.  For the last two decades,  two positions  have been used to read approximately  500
  meters  a piece.  While  the number  of meters  has remained  fairly  constant  at 14,300  over
  that time period,  it is a fair question  to explore  and, if needed,  have a discussion  during  the
  upcoming  budget  process  for Fiscal  Year 2024-25.

  7.  Clear  debris  near meters.  Finally,  we have begun  to replace  or dig out meter  boxes  that
  may be full  of debris.  The Water  Division  will  likely  be engaging  a third  party  to assist
  with  this  function.  Our goal  is to eliminate  possibilities  that may  be interfering  with  a
  Water  Meter  Reader's  ability  to observe  and record  a register  dial  reading  easily  and
  efficiently.
